facts.value: Annual Report on Treasury Management Activity and Actual Prudential Indicators for the financial year ended 31 March 2026, to Full Council on Thursday 16 July 2026 as Agenda Item 7b, as recommended by Audit and Standards Committee. Six-page covering report with five appendices listed on p1: A Temporary Investments 2025-26, B PWLB Loan Schedule 2025-26, C Actual Prudential Indicators, D Explanation of the Prudential Indicators, E The Economy and Interest Rates 2025-26. Held on disk: main report (doc 20531), Appendix C (doc 20534) and Appendix D (doc 20535). Appendices A, B and E not held. Report Author is Joseph Abbey, Principal Accountant (joseph.abbey@stroud.gov.uk / 01453 754133). Lead Director is Kathy O'Leary, Chief Executive. Financial Implications sign-off is Lucy Clothier, Strategic Head of Finance (lucy.clothier@stroud.gov.uk / 01453 754343). Legal sign-off is One Legal (shared legal service). MUFG named as treasury advisor at para 2.6.2. Read in full from local PDFs on 2026-08-16.

facts.value: TIES EXACTLY ON PRINCIPAL. Our file at 2026-03-31 for borrower STROUD DISTRICT COUNCIL: 18 loans, £100,717,000 principal, weighted rate 3.4489%, all 18 MATURITY loans (no EIP, no annuity). Paper Table 4 (p4) and Table 5 (p5) both give External Borrowing / Long-term (PWLB) at £100,717,000 — principal ties to the pound. Table 5 shows zero drawings and zero repayments in the year, so the same £100.717m ties at 1 April 2025 as well. Loan count, per-loan schedule and weighted rate sit in Appendix B (PWLB Loan Schedule 2025-26) which we do not have on disk, so the count and weighted rate cannot be cross-checked against theirs — only the principal is available in the body. Safe to quote in the email as '18 PWLB loans totalling £100,717,000' — count is ours, principal ties. Maturity profile from our file: 5-10y one loan £6.000m at 3.320%; 10-25y five loans £38.000m at 3.502%; 25y+ twelve loans £56.717m at 3.427%. No loans mature inside 5 years.

facts.note: Strongest form the check takes without Appendix B in hand. Principal ties to the pound and the book was static all year — nothing drawn, nothing repaid, nothing matured. Long-dated HRA-settlement shape from 2012 dominates: 56.7% of the book (£56.7m) is at 25y+.

facts.value: CHECKED. Using main body Table 4 (p4): CFR £136,674 - External £100,717 - LT Leases £433 - ST Leases £212 = £35,312 internal borrowing — TIES EXACTLY to Table 4's stated internal-borrowing line. Appendix D §5 (p1) restates the identity in words with the same £35.312m answer, though the wording only subtracts £0.433m of leases from the £136.674m CFR (would arithmetically give £35.524m) — the £35.312m result requires the full £645k of leases (both LT £433 and ST £212). Cosmetic wording issue in Appendix D, not an arithmetic error. Note: Appendix C separately reports CFR at 31 March 2026 as £131.519m rather than £136.674m — a £5.155m unexplained gap between Appendix C and the main body/Appendix D within the same paper. Not raised externally; recorded internally.

source.title: Table 4 main body (p4); Appendix D §5 (doc 20535, p1); Appendix C table (doc 20534, p1)

facts.note: Identity closes clean on the main body's own numbers. Two internal inconsistencies (£5.155m CFR gap between main body and Appendix C; three different figures £615, £645, £992 for other long-term liabilities) are not raised — pointing out cosmetic inconsistencies to an S151 in a first contact is off-scope for us and would read as pedantic.

facts.value: PWLB book did not move a pound in 2025-26 (Table 5, p5): Long-term (PWLB) opening £100,717k, increase £0, decrease £0, closing £100,717k. Zero drawings, zero repayments, zero maturities. Other long-term liabilities (IFRS 16 leases) moved £119k on run-off. The CFR grew by roughly £10m (Table 4, p4: £126,622k to £136,674k) and the whole increase was absorbed by internal borrowing (£25,166k to £35,312k, +£10,146k). Cash balances fell -£5,458k (Table 1: £44,450k to £38,992k) and investment portfolio fell -£4,898k (Table 3: £43,032k to £38,134k) — net cash-side draw funding the CFR growth. Zero new external borrowing throughout the year is a deliberate stance, consistent with §2.6.4's observation that Bank Rate fell from 4.50% at April 2025 to 3.75% by December 2025.
facts.note: This is the shape of the year: a static long-dated book with the whole CFR growth funded from cash. Similar in shape to Southend, South Ribble and Chorley in the pipeline batch — the district pattern where the treasury team sits on the pre-2012 HRA-settlement book and refuses to add long-dated PWLB at current rates. Fair to note in the email.

facts.value: Paper §2.6.4 (p3, verbatim): 'In February 2025, the Treasury Management Strategy forecast that interest rates would fall to 4.00% by September 25 and further to 3.75% by March 2026. The Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee set the base rate at 4.50% in May 2025, before reducing it to 4.00% in August 2025. By December 2025, the rate had been lowered to 3.75%, where it remained through to March 2026, in line with the Treasury Strategy.' The forecast was directionally correct and quantitatively close: the actual path reached 4.00% one month earlier than forecast (August rather than September 2025) and 3.75% three months earlier (December rather than March 2026), holding at 3.75% through year end — the same terminal rate they forecast. Unusually accurate against the strategies we have read for the same window (many overshot either the pace of cuts or the destination — see notes on Bedford, North East Lincolnshire, York, Buckinghamshire).
facts.note: This is the standout compliment. The template guidance is that the strongest openings are ones where the council did us a favour or got something right (Shropshire caught the April turn; Leicestershire let us test our engine). Stroud made a specific dated forecast fifteen months before the outturn and effectively hit it. Leading with this in the email is the honest read.

summary.text:
Six-page Annual Treasury Management Activity Report for the financial year ended 31 March 2026, to Full Council on 16 July 2026 as Agenda Item 7b (recommended by Audit and Standards Committee). Held on disk: main report doc 20531, Appendix C (Actual Prudential Indicators) doc 20534, Appendix D (Explanation of the Prudential Indicators) doc 20535. Appendices A (Temporary Investments), B (PWLB Loan Schedule) and E (Economy) are listed on p1 but not on disk. Report Author is Joseph Abbey, Principal Accountant; Financial sign-off is Lucy Clothier, Strategic Head of Finance — the S151 title is not stated in this paper so we take Lucy's title verbatim.

The PWLB loan-book reconciliation ties on principal: our file at 31 March 2026 returns 18 loans totalling £100,717,000 at a weighted 3.4489%, all MATURITY, against Table 4/5 of the paper which give External Borrowing / Long-term (PWLB) of £100,717,000. Principal ties to the pound. The loan schedule sits in Appendix B (not held) so the loan count and weighted rate can't be cross-checked against theirs — only the principal is in the body. Table 5 confirms zero drawings and zero repayments in the year, so the same principal ties at 1 April 2025 as well.

The balance-sheet identity closes exactly on the main body's numbers: CFR £136.674m less external £100.717m less LT leases £433k less ST leases £212k = £35.312m internal borrowing, tying Table 4's stated line. Two internal inconsistencies are noted for the file but not raised externally — Appendix C reports CFR at £131.519m rather than the main body's £136.674m (£5.155m unexplained gap), and the paper reports 'other long term liabilities' three different ways for the same date (Table 5 £615k, Table 4 £645k, Appendix C £992k). Neither affects the substance; both would read as pedantic in a first-contact email.

The distinctive shape of the year is that the PWLB book did not move a pound. Table 5 shows zero drawings, zero repayments, zero maturities. Meanwhile CFR grew about £10m (£126.622m to £136.674m on Table 4) and every pound of that growth was absorbed by internal borrowing (£25.166m to £35.312m, +£10.146m). Cash fell £5.458m and the investment portfolio fell £4.898m — the entire CFR uplift funded from cash rather than new PWLB. That is a deliberate stance, consistent with the base rate path §2.6.4 records (4.50% at April 2025 down to 3.75% by December 2025).

The standout compliment is the rate forecast at §2.6.4. In February 2025 the TMSS forecast base rate falling to 4.00% by September 2025 and 3.75% by March 2026. Actual: 4.00% August 2025 (one month early), 3.75% December 2025 (three months early), held to year end. Same terminal, essentially the same path — unusually accurate against the strategies we've read for the same window. Leading with this is the honest opening.

Indicative break-cost position: 18 of 18 loans below par with a curve-derived discount of £25.367m (25.2% of principal), against DMO notice 314/26 PM dated 2026-08-14. Largest discounts on the 30-35y bucket (PW500720/725 at 3.48% coupon, £10m and £9.717m). INDICATIVE only — only the DMO can quote. Framed in the note and email as a fact off the curve, not advice.

Stroud is HRA-dominated (HRA CFR £110.427m = 84% of the £131.519m CFR shown in Appendix C). HRA financing-costs-to-revenue ratio is 12.44% (inside the 15.72% indicator by a comfortable margin, stable against 12.49% in 2024/25). Investment portfolio £38.134m earning a temporary yield of 4.25% and a long-term yield of 1.56% (Table 2) — the long-term drag is the Lothbury and Hermes property funds in wind-down, with capital losses funded from the Investment Risk Earmarked Reserve so no GF hit. All prudential indicators held; £43.3m of headroom against the £145m Authorised Limit.

officer.body:
Hi Lucy,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Annual Treasury Management Report you took to Council on 16 July as Item 7b, ahead of the Q1 report your paragraph 1.6.2 flags for Audit and Standards on the same September pattern as last year. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your paper's ticking along neatly and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The cross-check first, which is where we always start. Our file holds eighteen PWLB loans for Stroud totalling £100,717,000 at a weighted 3.4489%, all maturity-type. Your Table 4 and Table 5 both give the external PWLB figure as £100,717,000 — that agrees to the pound. Table 5 also shows no drawings and no repayments in the year, so the opening at 1 April 2025 ties as well. Your per-loan schedule sits in your Appendix B, which we don't hold, so we can't line-check the count or the weighted rate against yours; only the principal is in the body of the paper we read.

What first caught our eye is your paragraph 2.6.4. Fifteen months ago in the February 2025 Strategy you forecast the base rate falling to 4.00% by September 2025 and 3.75% by March 2026. The paper then records the actual path: 4.00% in August 2025, so one month early, and 3.75% by December 2025, three months early, held there through year end. Same terminal, essentially the same path. We've read a lot of strategies for the same window and most of them overshot in one direction or the other — either forecasting faster cuts that didn't come or missing the destination. Being that close to right on a fifteen-month forecast is unusual and worth saying.

The distinctive shape of the year is what happened around that: your PWLB book didn't move a pound. Zero drawings, zero repayments, zero maturities. Meanwhile the CFR on your Table 4 grew about £10m — from £126.622m to £136.674m — and every pound of that increase was absorbed by internal borrowing, which rose from £25.166m to £35.312m. Cash balances (Table 1) fell £5.458m over the same year. That's a deliberate stance and it reads directly against the falling base rate path you forecast: choosing not to fix new long-dated PWLB while shorter-dated cash carried the CFR growth. The identity ties exactly on your own numbers — CFR £136.674m less external £100.717m less £645k of leases equals your £35.312m — which is the reason the shape is worth naming, because it stands up under its own arithmetic.
